opening.text: Imagine a young man who borrowed a large sum of money. He meant to pay it back. But life got hard, and the debt grew. One day the lender came to his door. The man had nothing to give. He knew what the law allowed. He could lose everything.

Then a friend stepped into the room. He had heard about the trouble. He said to the lender, I will pay it. Every bit. The lender took the payment. The debt was gone. But the friend did not say, you are free to do as you wish. He said, now you owe it to me, and I will be kind about how you repay it.
That small story is not perfect. But it points to something true. We each carry a debt we cannot pay. And Someone has stepped in.
Today I want to speak about the Atonement of Jesus Christ. It is the center of our faith, and it is the greatest act of love in all of history.

mainMessage.text: The Atonement is the way Jesus Christ took on Himself our sins, our pains, and even death, so that we could be forgiven, healed, and raised up. It is not a distant idea. It reaches into everyday life. It meets us when we make a mistake. It meets us when we are hurt by someone else. And it meets us at the grave.
We do not earn it. We receive it. And as we receive it, we are changed.

We will look at six parts. First, why we need a Savior. Second, what He suffered. Third, who it was for. Fourth, how it heals and changes us. Fifth, how mercy and justice meet. And sixth, the peace it brings.

blocks.text: Let us begin with an honest question. Why do we need a Savior at all? Paul gave a short answer.
For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;
All. That word includes you and me. No one gets through life without mistakes. Some are small. Some are heavy. But all of us fall short.
The Book of Mormon teaches that the problem is bigger than our mistakes. It reaches to death itself.

Wherefore, it must needs be an infinite atonement—save it should be an infinite atonement this corruption could not put on incorruption. Wherefore, the first judgment which came upon man must needs have remained to an endless duration. And if so, this flesh must have laid down to rot and to crumble to its mother earth, to rise no more.

Without an infinite atonement, death would have been the end. Our bodies would never rise. Our spirits would be lost. Jacob wanted his people to see how great the need was. Only an infinite sacrifice could answer an infinite problem.

Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained why we cannot fix this ourselves. In his talk "The Atonement Can Secure Your Peace and Happiness," from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

Justice . . . requires that every broken law be satisfied. When you obey the laws of God, you are blessed, but there is no additional credit earned that can be saved to satisfy the laws that you break. If not resolved, broken laws can cause your life to be miserable and would keep you from returning to God.

There is no extra credit that can be saved. Think about that. Even a good life does not cancel a past mistake. Our good deeds are needed, but they cannot pay the debt. That is why the friend in our story mattered so much. Someone else had to pay what we could not.
What did the Savior do to pay it? Isaiah saw it seven hundred years before He came.

Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
Borne our griefs. Carried our sorrows. This was not an act from a distance. He took our pain into Himself. Then, in our own day, He described it to Joseph Smith in His own words.
To tremble because of pain. To bleed at every pore. He asked that the cup might pass. And then He drank it. Why? Because He loved the Father and He loved us.
Elder Joseph B. Wirthlin of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles described what this gift accomplished. In his talk "Christians in Belief and Action," from the October 1996 general conference, he said:

The Atonement of Jesus Christ, an act of pure love, overcame the effects of the Fall and provided the way for all mankind to return to the presence of God. As part of the Atonement, the Savior overcame physical death and provided immortality for every one of God's children through the Resurrection. He also overcame spiritual death and provided the possibility of eternal life, the life that God lives and the greatest of all the gifts of God.

An act of pure love. Not a duty done coldly. It was love. The friend in our story did not pay the debt to feel important. He did it because he cared. Our Savior did the same, on a scale we can barely picture.
Who was this gift for? The answer is every single one of us.
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
The word is world. Not a few. Not the righteous only. The whole world. And Nephi said it again in his own way.

He doeth not anything save it be for the benefit of the world; for he loveth the world, even that he layeth down his own life that he may draw all men unto him. Wherefore, he commandeth none that they shall not partake of his salvation.
He commandeth none that they shall not partake. The invitation is open to all. No one is left out.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke of this reach. In his talk "All Men Everywhere," from the April 2006 general conference, he said:

These teachings that the resurrecting and cleansing power of the Atonement is for all contradict the assertion that the grace of God saves only a chosen few. His grace is for all. These teachings of the Book of Mormon expand our vision and enlarge our understanding of the all-encompassing love of God and the universal effect of His Atonement for all men everywhere.
His grace is for all. If you have ever wondered whether you are included, here is your answer. You are. The friend in our story paid for a debtor he knew by name. And the Savior knows your name.
The Atonement does more than erase the past. It heals us and changes us. Alma told the people of Gideon how far it reaches.

And he shall go forth, suffering pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind; and this that the word might be fulfilled which saith he will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people.
And he will take upon him death, that he may loose the bands of death which bind his people; and he will take upon him their infirmities, that his bowels may be filled with mercy, according to the flesh, that he may know according to the flesh how to succor his people according to their infirmities.
Pains, afflictions, temptations, sicknesses, death, infirmities. Alma lists it all. The Savior understands. He took it upon Himself so that He would know how to help us.

Elder David A. Bednar of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught that the Atonement is for more than the wrongdoer. In his talk "Clean Hands and a Pure Heart," from the October 2007 general conference, he said:

It is the Atonement of Jesus Christ that provides both a cleansing and redeeming power that helps us to overcome sin and a sanctifying and strengthening power that helps us to become better than we ever could by relying only upon our own strength. The infinite Atonement is for both the sinner and for the saint in each of us.
Both the sinner and the saint in each of us. That is a kind thought. The friend in our story paid the debt, but the Savior goes further. He also gives strength so that we can walk a new road.
A question that has puzzled many people is this. If God is merciful, why must there be a sacrifice? Alma answered it for his son Corianton.

And thus he shall bring salvation to all those who shall believe on his name; this being the intent of this last sacrifice, to bring about the bowels of mercy, which overpowereth justice, and bringeth about means unto men that they may have faith unto repentance.
And thus mercy can satisfy the demands of justice, and encircles them in the arms of safety, while he that exercises no faith unto repentance is exposed to the whole law of the demands of justice; therefore only unto him that has faith unto repentance is brought about the great and eternal plan of redemption.
Mercy does not cancel justice. Mercy satisfies it. The debt is truly paid. And those who turn to Christ with faith unto repentance are held in the arms of safety.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said it plainly. In his article "Moral Agency," in the June 2009 Ensign, he wrote:

We need a Savior, a Mediator who can overcome the effects of our sins and errors so that they are not necessarily fatal. It is because of the Atonement of Christ that we can recover from bad choices and be justified under the law as if we had not sinned.
Not necessarily fatal. That is the hope. Our sins and errors do not have to be the end of the story. In our little tale, the lender is satisfied and the man is free. Free to start again.
What does all of this give us? Peace. The Savior promised it to His disciples on the night before He suffered.
Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
He said this knowing what lay ahead. And He added more.
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
In the world ye shall have tribulation. He does not hide that. But in Him, we have peace. I have overcome the world. That is the victory of the Atonement.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency gave hope to anyone who feels they have gone too far. In his talk "The Point of Safe Return," from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

Christ came to save us. If we have taken a wrong course, the Atonement of Jesus Christ can give us the assurance that sin is not a point of no return. A safe return is possible if we will follow God's plan for our salvation.
A safe return is possible. Whatever you have done, whatever you carry, there is a way back. It was paid for.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time they felt the Atonement lift a burden. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Alma remembers Jesus Christ

blocks.text: Alma the Younger had fought against the Church. An angel stopped him. For three days he lay in pain, remembering every wrong thing he had done. He felt he could not be forgiven. Then he remembered what his father had taught him.

And it came to pass that as I was thus racked with torment, while I was harrowed up by the memory of my many sins, behold, I remembered also to have heard my father prophesy unto the people concerning the coming of one Jesus Christ, a Son of God, to atone for the sins of the world.
Now, as my mind caught hold upon this thought, I cried within my heart: O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me, who am in the gall of bitterness, and am encircled about by the everlasting chains of death.
And now, behold, when I thought this, I could remember my pains no more; yea, I was harrowed up by the memory of my sins no more.
He did not have a long prayer. He had one thought, and one cry. And the Savior answered. The pain was gone. The debt was paid. Alma stood up a new man.

application.text: Here are some steps for this week.
First, name the debt. Think of something you have been carrying that you cannot fix on your own. Write it down. Then kneel and give it to the Savior in prayer.
Second, receive the payment. If you are repenting of something, do not keep paying for it with guilt. Ask the Lord to forgive you, and then believe that He has.
Third, thank Him. Spend a few minutes this week thanking the Savior for His Atonement. Be specific. Tell Him what it has meant to you.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ is my Savior and my Redeemer. I know that He suffered for my sins and my sorrows. I know that He paid a debt I could not pay. I have felt His mercy, and I know that it is real. I know that because of Him, we can be forgiven, healed, and raised up. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

versions.analogy: A debt paid by a friend

opening.text: Somewhere in the mountains there is a canyon so wide that no one can jump it. On one side is where you are. On the other side is where you want to be. You can walk to the edge and look across. You can wish. You can even try to build a ladder of good intentions. But the gap is too wide, and the drop is too deep.
Now picture a bridge. Someone built it, at great cost, and left it open for all. You do not have to build it. You only have to walk across.
That is how I think of the Atonement of Jesus Christ. There is a gap between us and God. We could not close it. He did. And the bridge is open today.

mainMessage.text: The Atonement is the work of the Savior in Gethsemane and on the cross, and His rising from the tomb. Through it, He took on our sins, our pain, and our death. Through it, we can be forgiven, made whole, and brought back into the presence of God.
It is a gift. It was given freely. But it asks something of us. We must cross the bridge. We must have faith, repent, and follow Him.

Together we will look at six things. First, the gap itself. Second, the price of the bridge. Third, who may cross. Fourth, how the bridge heals those who walk it. Fifth, how mercy and justice are both kept. And sixth, the peace on the far side.

blocks.text: Paul described the gap in one line.
For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;
Come short. Like a jumper who leaps with all her strength and still lands short of the other side. That is every one of us. Even our best effort falls short.
Jacob taught that the gap includes death.

Wherefore, it must needs be an infinite atonement—save it should be an infinite atonement this corruption could not put on incorruption. Wherefore, the first judgment which came upon man must needs have remained to an endless duration. And if so, this flesh must have laid down to rot and to crumble to its mother earth, to rise no more.
If there were no bridge, the body would lie in the grave forever. But the bridge is infinite. Its reach extends past death.

Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained why we cannot cross by ourselves. In his talk "The Atonement Can Secure Your Peace and Happiness," from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

Justice . . . requires that every broken law be satisfied. When you obey the laws of God, you are blessed, but there is no additional credit earned that can be saved to satisfy the laws that you break. If not resolved, broken laws can cause your life to be miserable and would keep you from returning to God.
Good works are the steps we take on the bridge. They matter. But they do not build the bridge. Only Jesus Christ could do that.
What did the bridge cost? Isaiah described it.

Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
He was wounded for our transgressions. The beams of that bridge were His suffering. And in our day, He told us what it was like.
He did not want to drink the bitter cup. And still He did. Nevertheless, glory be to the Father. That is the heart of obedience and love together.
Elder Joseph B. Wirthlin of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave a clear summary. In his talk "Christians in Belief and Action," from the October 1996 general conference, he said:

The Atonement of Jesus Christ, an act of pure love, overcame the effects of the Fall and provided the way for all mankind to return to the presence of God. As part of the Atonement, the Savior overcame physical death and provided immortality for every one of God's children through the Resurrection. He also overcame spiritual death and provided the possibility of eternal life, the life that God lives and the greatest of all the gifts of God.
The way for all mankind to return. That is what a bridge is. It is the way across. And He built it out of love.
The bridge is open to everyone. Jesus said so Himself.
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
Whosoever. A word with no fence around it. Nephi taught the same.

He doeth not anything save it be for the benefit of the world; for he loveth the world, even that he layeth down his own life that he may draw all men unto him. Wherefore, he commandeth none that they shall not partake of his salvation.
No toll booth. No guard at the entrance. He commandeth none that they shall not partake.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles reminded us of this wide reach. In his talk "All Men Everywhere," from the April 2006 general conference, he said:

These teachings that the resurrecting and cleansing power of the Atonement is for all contradict the assertion that the grace of God saves only a chosen few. His grace is for all. These teachings of the Book of Mormon expand our vision and enlarge our understanding of the all-encompassing love of God and the universal effect of His Atonement for all men everywhere.
For all men everywhere. If you are standing on the edge and wondering if the bridge is for you, it is. He built it with you in mind.
A good bridge does more than carry us over. This one changes the traveler.

And he shall go forth, suffering pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind; and this that the word might be fulfilled which saith he will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people.
And he will take upon him death, that he may loose the bands of death which bind his people; and he will take upon him their infirmities, that his bowels may be filled with mercy, according to the flesh, that he may know according to the flesh how to succor his people according to their infirmities.
He walked every hard road first. That is why He knows how to help us. He took our sicknesses and our weakness so that He could understand them from the inside.
Elder David A. Bednar of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained the double gift. In his talk "Clean Hands and a Pure Heart," from the October 2007 general conference, he said:

It is the Atonement of Jesus Christ that provides both a cleansing and redeeming power that helps us to overcome sin and a sanctifying and strengthening power that helps us to become better than we ever could by relying only upon our own strength. The infinite Atonement is for both the sinner and for the saint in each of us.
Cleansing and strengthening. As we cross, we are washed and we are given strength. The one who arrives on the far side is not the same person who started.
Some ask how God can be both perfectly just and perfectly merciful. Alma explained that to his son.

And thus he shall bring salvation to all those who shall believe on his name; this being the intent of this last sacrifice, to bring about the bowels of mercy, which overpowereth justice, and bringeth about means unto men that they may have faith unto repentance.
And thus mercy can satisfy the demands of justice, and encircles them in the arms of safety, while he that exercises no faith unto repentance is exposed to the whole law of the demands of justice; therefore only unto him that has faith unto repentance is brought about the great and eternal plan of redemption.

The bridge honors the law. Justice is not ignored; it is met by the Savior's sacrifice. And mercy is then free to reach us. Those who cross with faith unto repentance are encircled in the arms of safety.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles wrote about what this means for us. In his article "Moral Agency," in the June 2009 Ensign, he said:

We need a Savior, a Mediator who can overcome the effects of our sins and errors so that they are not necessarily fatal. It is because of the Atonement of Christ that we can recover from bad choices and be justified under the law as if we had not sinned.
We can recover. That is the word to remember. A fall at the edge of a canyon is final. A fall on a bridge can be recovered from, if we get back up and keep walking.
On the far side of the bridge, there is peace. Jesus promised it.
Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
Not as the world giveth. The world gives peace that depends on circumstances. His peace stays in the storm.
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
Be of good cheer. He says this to people who will still face hard days. He has overcome. And we can walk with Him.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency spoke to those who think they have gone too far. In his talk "The Point of Safe Return," from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

Christ came to save us. If we have taken a wrong course, the Atonement of Jesus Christ can give us the assurance that sin is not a point of no return. A safe return is possible if we will follow God's plan for our salvation.
No point of no return. The bridge is still there. You can step back onto it any day.

story.title: The thief on the cross

blocks.text: On the day Jesus was crucified, two men hung beside Him. One of them had done wrong and knew it. He looked at the Savior and said something short and honest.

And he said unto Jesus, Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.
And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.
The man had no time left. He had no way to make up for what he had done. But he turned to Jesus, and Jesus answered at once. To day. The bridge is that near. It is never too late to step onto it.

application.text: Here are some steps for this week.
First, find your edge. Is there a gap between you and God that you have felt? Name it in prayer. Tell Him honestly where you are.
Second, take one step. Choose one act of faith. Read a chapter about the Savior. Make a call to someone you need to forgive. Take the step.
Third, help someone cross. Think of one person who feels far from God. Reach out with a kind word, a message, or an invitation to church.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ lives. I know that He built the way back to our Father in Heaven, and that He did it with His own life. I have felt His hand help me when I could not help myself. I know that the bridge is open to every one of us. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: A lifeguard watches the water all day. Most days nothing happens. But on one hot afternoon, a swimmer goes out too far and gets caught in a current. She tries to swim back. The harder she kicks, the farther she drifts. She is tired, and she is afraid.
Then a rope lands beside her. Someone has thrown a lifeline. She does not have to swim any more. She only has to hold on, and let herself be pulled in.
That is the best picture I know of the Atonement. We are not strong enough to save ourselves from sin and death. But a lifeline has been thrown. All we need to do is take hold.

mainMessage.text: The Atonement of Jesus Christ is the greatest rescue ever made. He went into the deepest water so that no one would have to stay there alone. Through Him, our sins can be forgiven. Our pain can be healed. And death is not the end.
It is not a reward for the strong. It is help for the drowning. Every one of us qualifies.

We will think about six things today. First, why we cannot save ourselves. Second, what the rescue cost Him. Third, how far the rope reaches. Fourth, how it lifts and then strengthens us. Fifth, how mercy and justice work together. And sixth, the calm that follows.

blocks.text: The water we are in is described by Paul.
For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;
Notice the word all. This is not about a few reckless swimmers. All of us have been out of our depth at some point.
Jacob added that even our bodies need rescue.

Wherefore, it must needs be an infinite atonement—save it should be an infinite atonement this corruption could not put on incorruption. Wherefore, the first judgment which came upon man must needs have remained to an endless duration. And if so, this flesh must have laid down to rot and to crumble to its mother earth, to rise no more.
An infinite atonement. A rescue large enough to reach past the grave. Nothing smaller would do.

Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles described why swimming harder does not work. In his talk "The Atonement Can Secure Your Peace and Happiness," from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

Justice . . . requires that every broken law be satisfied. When you obey the laws of God, you are blessed, but there is no additional credit earned that can be saved to satisfy the laws that you break. If not resolved, broken laws can cause your life to be miserable and would keep you from returning to God.
No extra credit. You cannot swim out of this current with good deeds alone. Good deeds are important, but what we need most is the rope.
Lifelines are not free. Someone has to go into danger to throw them. Isaiah saw the cost.

Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
By his stripes we are healed. The Savior took the wounds so that we would not have to.
He later told us how deep He went.
Would that I might not drink the bitter cup. This was not easy for Him. He felt it all. And still He finished.
Elder Joseph B. Wirthlin of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said what moved Him. In his talk "Christians in Belief and Action," from the October 1996 general conference, he said:

The Atonement of Jesus Christ, an act of pure love, overcame the effects of the Fall and provided the way for all mankind to return to the presence of God. As part of the Atonement, the Savior overcame physical death and provided immortality for every one of God's children through the Resurrection. He also overcame spiritual death and provided the possibility of eternal life, the life that God lives and the greatest of all the gifts of God.
An act of pure love. The Savior was not forced into the water. He went in because He loved the swimmer.
How far does the rope reach? Farther than we may think.
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
Should not perish. Whoever believes may hold the line and be pulled to safety.

He doeth not anything save it be for the benefit of the world; for he loveth the world, even that he layeth down his own life that he may draw all men unto him. Wherefore, he commandeth none that they shall not partake of his salvation.
Draw all men unto him. A rope is for drawing in. His whole purpose is to bring us close.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles testified of its reach. In his talk "All Men Everywhere," from the April 2006 general conference, he said:

These teachings that the resurrecting and cleansing power of the Atonement is for all contradict the assertion that the grace of God saves only a chosen few. His grace is for all. These teachings of the Book of Mormon expand our vision and enlarge our understanding of the all-encompassing love of God and the universal effect of His Atonement for all men everywhere.
His grace is for all. There is no swimmer too far out. The rope is long enough.
Once the swimmer is pulled in, the lifeguard does not leave her on the sand. He wraps her in a towel and makes sure she is warm. The Atonement does the same.

And he shall go forth, suffering pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind; and this that the word might be fulfilled which saith he will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people.
And he will take upon him death, that he may loose the bands of death which bind his people; and he will take upon him their infirmities, that his bowels may be filled with mercy, according to the flesh, that he may know according to the flesh how to succor his people according to their infirmities.
To succor means to run to help. He knows how to run to us because He has felt what we feel.

Elder David A. Bednar of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said the rescue goes further than forgiveness. In his talk "Clean Hands and a Pure Heart," from the October 2007 general conference, he said:

It is the Atonement of Jesus Christ that provides both a cleansing and redeeming power that helps us to overcome sin and a sanctifying and strengthening power that helps us to become better than we ever could by relying only upon our own strength. The infinite Atonement is for both the sinner and for the saint in each of us.
A strengthening power. After the rescue, He helps us learn to swim. He does not leave us as we were.
Why did it take a sacrifice? Alma explained the balance.

And thus he shall bring salvation to all those who shall believe on his name; this being the intent of this last sacrifice, to bring about the bowels of mercy, which overpowereth justice, and bringeth about means unto men that they may have faith unto repentance.
And thus mercy can satisfy the demands of justice, and encircles them in the arms of safety, while he that exercises no faith unto repentance is exposed to the whole law of the demands of justice; therefore only unto him that has faith unto repentance is brought about the great and eternal plan of redemption.
The arms of safety. That is what holds us when we hold the rope. Justice is met. Mercy is free. And we are held.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles wrote what this gives us. In his article "Moral Agency," in the June 2009 Ensign, he said:

We need a Savior, a Mediator who can overcome the effects of our sins and errors so that they are not necessarily fatal. It is because of the Atonement of Christ that we can recover from bad choices and be justified under the law as if we had not sinned.
Not necessarily fatal. A drowning is fatal, but not when there is a rescue. Our mistakes need not be the end.
After the rescue, there is calm. The Savior promised it.
Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
Neither let it be afraid. The panic of the water gives way to a deep quiet.
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
He does not say the sea will be calm. He says He has overcome it. We can face the waves because we are tied to the One who can master them.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency gave this encouragement. In his talk "The Point of Safe Return," from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

Christ came to save us. If we have taken a wrong course, the Atonement of Jesus Christ can give us the assurance that sin is not a point of no return. A safe return is possible if we will follow God's plan for our salvation.
A safe return. The shore is not far. Hold on.

story.title: The woman caught in sin

blocks.text: A woman was brought to Jesus by men who wanted to see her punished. They stood around her with stones in their hands. Jesus told them that whoever was without sin should throw the first stone. One by one, they left. At last she stood alone with the Savior.

When Jesus had lifted up himself, and saw none but the woman, he said unto her, Woman, where are those thine accusers? hath no man condemned thee?
She said, No man, Lord. And Jesus said unto her, Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.

She had been in deep water, and He pulled her out. Neither do I condemn thee. And then He gave her a new start. Go, and sin no more. That is the whole pattern of rescue. He lifts us, and then He points us forward.

application.text: Here are some steps for this week.
First, hold the rope. Pray each day this week and say, Father, I need help, and I take hold of Thy Son. Do it in your own words.
Second, let go of the swim. Stop trying to earn your way out of a mistake. Repent, make right what you can, and trust the Savior with the rest.
Third, throw a line. Think of someone who may be struggling. Send them a note or call. Let them know someone cares.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ is my Redeemer. I know that He rescues all who turn to Him. I have felt His hand lift me out of dark places, and I know that He will do the same for everyone. I know that He lives, and that His Atonement is real. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: My father once had a coat he loved. It was old and well made. One day it caught on a nail and tore along the shoulder. He could have thrown it out. Instead, he took it to a tailor. The tailor did not hide the tear. He stitched it so carefully that when the work was done, the coat was stronger at that spot than anywhere else.

I have thought about that coat many times. It says something about how the Savior treats us. We tear. We catch ourselves on things. But He does not throw us out. He mends us, and often we come back stronger.
That mending has a name. It is the Atonement of Jesus Christ.

mainMessage.text: The Atonement is the Savior's act of taking on Himself the sins, pains, and sorrows of all people, and then overcoming death. It is how we are forgiven. It is how we are healed. It is how we are raised.
It is also personal. It was done for you. When you feel torn or worn, the same hands that mended the world can mend you.

We will look at six things. First, the tear we all carry. Second, the hands that did the mending. Third, whom He mends. Fourth, how He makes us stronger. Fifth, how mercy and justice are woven together. And sixth, the peace of a coat well mended.

blocks.text: The tear is in all of us. Paul put it simply.
For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;
All have sinned. This is not meant to shame us. It is meant to help us see why we need the tailor.
Jacob taught how deep the damage goes.

Wherefore, it must needs be an infinite atonement—save it should be an infinite atonement this corruption could not put on incorruption. Wherefore, the first judgment which came upon man must needs have remained to an endless duration. And if so, this flesh must have laid down to rot and to crumble to its mother earth, to rise no more.
The cloth of mortal life wears out. Without an infinite atonement, there would be no repair. But Jacob taught that there is one.

Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said we cannot patch it ourselves. In his talk "The Atonement Can Secure Your Peace and Happiness," from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

Justice . . . requires that every broken law be satisfied. When you obey the laws of God, you are blessed, but there is no additional credit earned that can be saved to satisfy the laws that you break. If not resolved, broken laws can cause your life to be miserable and would keep you from returning to God.
Good habits are like caring for the coat. They keep it in better shape. But they do not undo a tear that has already happened. For that we need the mender.
Whose hands did the mending, and what did it cost? Isaiah described it long before.

Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
With his stripes we are healed. His hands took the injury so that ours could be repaired.
He told us of it in this dispensation.
I partook and finished. He did not stop at the hardest moment. He completed the work.
Elder Joseph B. Wirthlin of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said what drove it. In his talk "Christians in Belief and Action," from the October 1996 general conference, he said:

The Atonement of Jesus Christ, an act of pure love, overcame the effects of the Fall and provided the way for all mankind to return to the presence of God. As part of the Atonement, the Savior overcame physical death and provided immortality for every one of God's children through the Resurrection. He also overcame spiritual death and provided the possibility of eternal life, the life that God lives and the greatest of all the gifts of God.
Pure love. A tailor who loved the coat would not rush. The Savior loved us enough to finish every stitch.
Whom does He mend? Everyone who brings themselves to Him.
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
Whosoever. No coat is too old or too torn to be taken in.

He doeth not anything save it be for the benefit of the world; for he loveth the world, even that he layeth down his own life that he may draw all men unto him. Wherefore, he commandeth none that they shall not partake of his salvation.
He commandeth none that they shall not partake. The shop is open to all.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles testified of this. In his talk "All Men Everywhere," from the April 2006 general conference, he said:

These teachings that the resurrecting and cleansing power of the Atonement is for all contradict the assertion that the grace of God saves only a chosen few. His grace is for all. These teachings of the Book of Mormon expand our vision and enlarge our understanding of the all-encompassing love of God and the universal effect of His Atonement for all men everywhere.
His grace is for all. There is no one He turns away at the door.
The repaired spot on my father's coat was stronger than before. The Atonement works that way too. It does more than patch.

And he shall go forth, suffering pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind; and this that the word might be fulfilled which saith he will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people.
And he will take upon him death, that he may loose the bands of death which bind his people; and he will take upon him their infirmities, that his bowels may be filled with mercy, according to the flesh, that he may know according to the flesh how to succor his people according to their infirmities.
He knows each weakness because He has taken it upon Himself. Nothing about our weakness surprises Him.
Elder David A. Bednar of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles described this strengthening. In his talk "Clean Hands and a Pure Heart," from the October 2007 general conference, he said:

It is the Atonement of Jesus Christ that provides both a cleansing and redeeming power that helps us to overcome sin and a sanctifying and strengthening power that helps us to become better than we ever could by relying only upon our own strength. The infinite Atonement is for both the sinner and for the saint in each of us.
Better than we ever could by our own strength. That is what a master mender gives. Not only a repair, but a stronger garment.
A good repair uses threads that hold. Alma showed how mercy and justice are woven together.

And thus he shall bring salvation to all those who shall believe on his name; this being the intent of this last sacrifice, to bring about the bowels of mercy, which overpowereth justice, and bringeth about means unto men that they may have faith unto repentance.
And thus mercy can satisfy the demands of justice, and encircles them in the arms of safety, while he that exercises no faith unto repentance is exposed to the whole law of the demands of justice; therefore only unto him that has faith unto repentance is brought about the great and eternal plan of redemption.
Mercy and justice are both honored. The Savior paid what justice required. Mercy then wraps us in safety. The repair is complete and honest.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles wrote about it in the June 2009 Ensign. In his article "Moral Agency," he said:

We need a Savior, a Mediator who can overcome the effects of our sins and errors so that they are not necessarily fatal. It is because of the Atonement of Christ that we can recover from bad choices and be justified under the law as if we had not sinned.
Recover. Be justified. As if we had not sinned. The coat is whole again.
A coat that has been mended well can be worn without worry. That is the peace the Savior promised.
Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
Let not your heart be troubled. He says it while knowing what He is about to endure for us.
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
We will still face rough weather. But we wear a coat that has been mended by the One who overcame the world.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency spoke to those who worry they are beyond repair. In his talk "The Point of Safe Return," from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

Christ came to save us. If we have taken a wrong course, the Atonement of Jesus Christ can give us the assurance that sin is not a point of no return. A safe return is possible if we will follow God's plan for our salvation.
Not beyond repair. Not past return. Come back to Him.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time they were welcomed back after going wrong. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The prodigal son comes home

blocks.text: Jesus told of a young man who took his inheritance and wasted it in a far country. When he had nothing left, he decided to go home. He rehearsed an apology on the way. He expected to be a servant.
And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.

The father saw him a great way off. That means he had been watching the road. He ran. He did not wait for the apology. He embraced his son, torn clothes and all. That is how our Father in Heaven receives us when we return to Him through His Son.

application.text: Here are some steps for this week.
First, bring the tear. Think of the place in your life that feels torn or weak. Take it to the Lord in prayer and ask Him to mend it.
Second, let it be strengthened. When something has been forgiven, do not keep picking at the stitch. Go forward and let the Lord make you stronger there.
Third, welcome someone back. Reach out to a person who has drifted. Be like the father on the road. Run to them.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ makes broken things whole. I have felt His mercy in places where I felt worn out and torn. I know that He loves each of us and that He has power to heal what we cannot. I know that He lives. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

opening.text: On a rocky shore, there is a boat stuck on the sand. It was left when the tide went out. The owner pushes and pulls. He puts his back into it. The boat does not move an inch. It is too heavy, and the ground holds it too firmly.
Then, hours later, the tide returns. No one pushes. No one pulls. The water simply rises, and the boat floats free. It is lifted by something far greater than the owner.
The Atonement of Jesus Christ is like that tide. We spend so much energy pushing against things we cannot move. And He comes in, like the sea, and lifts us.

mainMessage.text: The Atonement is the work by which Jesus Christ overcame sin and death for us. It is the heart of the gospel. It lifts what is stuck, heals what is hurt, and raises what has died.
We cannot do this work. But we can invite it. We can step into the water. We can let it carry us.

We will look at six things. First, how stuck we are without Him. Second, what the tide cost. Third, how far it reaches. Fourth, what it does for us once we are afloat. Fifth, how it satisfies both justice and mercy. And sixth, the calm water it brings.

blocks.text: How stuck are we? Paul wrote it plainly.
For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;
No one is exempt. Every one of us has tried to push the boat and found it heavy.
Jacob went further and spoke of death.

Wherefore, it must needs be an infinite atonement—save it should be an infinite atonement this corruption could not put on incorruption. Wherefore, the first judgment which came upon man must needs have remained to an endless duration. And if so, this flesh must have laid down to rot and to crumble to its mother earth, to rise no more.
Infinite. The tide that lifts us is not a pond. It is an ocean. Only something that great could move something this heavy.

Elder Richard G. Scott of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said why pushing alone fails. In his talk "The Atonement Can Secure Your Peace and Happiness," from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

Justice . . . requires that every broken law be satisfied. When you obey the laws of God, you are blessed, but there is no additional credit earned that can be saved to satisfy the laws that you break. If not resolved, broken laws can cause your life to be miserable and would keep you from returning to God.
Effort is good. We should push. But we should know that the lift will not come from us. It comes from Him.
What did it cost to bring in the tide? Isaiah described the price.

Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
He was wounded. He was bruised. The sea has a great weight, and He bore it.
And He told Joseph Smith what it was like.
He trembled. He bled. He wished He did not have to. And yet He finished. That is not a small act. That is the love of God at work.
Elder Joseph B. Wirthlin of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles described what He accomplished. In his talk "Christians in Belief and Action," from the October 1996 general conference, he said:

The Atonement of Jesus Christ, an act of pure love, overcame the effects of the Fall and provided the way for all mankind to return to the presence of God. As part of the Atonement, the Savior overcame physical death and provided immortality for every one of God's children through the Resurrection. He also overcame spiritual death and provided the possibility of eternal life, the life that God lives and the greatest of all the gifts of God.
Two deaths overcome. Physical and spiritual. The tide reaches both shores.
A tide does not choose which boats to lift. It reaches every shore. So does His love.
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
The world. That is a very wide shoreline. Nephi taught the same.

He doeth not anything save it be for the benefit of the world; for he loveth the world, even that he layeth down his own life that he may draw all men unto him. Wherefore, he commandeth none that they shall not partake of his salvation.
All men. None are commanded away. He draws everyone toward Him.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke of this wide reach. In his talk "All Men Everywhere," from the April 2006 general conference, he said:

These teachings that the resurrecting and cleansing power of the Atonement is for all contradict the assertion that the grace of God saves only a chosen few. His grace is for all. These teachings of the Book of Mormon expand our vision and enlarge our understanding of the all-encompassing love of God and the universal effect of His Atonement for all men everywhere.
No one is left on the sand. Not because of their past or their weakness. His grace is for all.
Once the boat floats, it can sail. The Atonement does not simply lift us. It makes us able to move.

And he shall go forth, suffering pains and afflictions and temptations of every kind; and this that the word might be fulfilled which saith he will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people.
And he will take upon him death, that he may loose the bands of death which bind his people; and he will take upon him their infirmities, that his bowels may be filled with mercy, according to the flesh, that he may know according to the flesh how to succor his people according to their infirmities.
He loosed the bands of death. The word bands is a good one. Bands hold a boat to the shore. He cut them. He also took our infirmities so that He could help us carry them.
Elder David A. Bednar of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said the Atonement helps us in two ways. In his talk "Clean Hands and a Pure Heart," from the October 2007 general conference, he said:

It is the Atonement of Jesus Christ that provides both a cleansing and redeeming power that helps us to overcome sin and a sanctifying and strengthening power that helps us to become better than we ever could by relying only upon our own strength. The infinite Atonement is for both the sinner and for the saint in each of us.
A cleansing power and a strengthening power. First He clears the hull. Then He fills the sails. We are not meant to float forever. We are meant to go somewhere.
Why did the tide need to come in this way? Alma taught his son about the law behind it.

And thus he shall bring salvation to all those who shall believe on his name; this being the intent of this last sacrifice, to bring about the bowels of mercy, which overpowereth justice, and bringeth about means unto men that they may have faith unto repentance.
And thus mercy can satisfy the demands of justice, and encircles them in the arms of safety, while he that exercises no faith unto repentance is exposed to the whole law of the demands of justice; therefore only unto him that has faith unto repentance is brought about the great and eternal plan of redemption.
The tide came in according to law. Justice was met. Mercy was extended. We are held in safety when we have faith unto repentance.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles wrote in the June 2009 Ensign. In his article "Moral Agency," he said:

We need a Savior, a Mediator who can overcome the effects of our sins and errors so that they are not necessarily fatal. It is because of the Atonement of Christ that we can recover from bad choices and be justified under the law as if we had not sinned.
A Mediator stands between us and the law, and carries us across. That is what the tide does. It does what we could not do alone.
When the water is calm and the boat floats, there is peace. The Savior promised it.
Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
My peace I give unto you. It is His own peace, the peace He had even as He went to Gethsemane.
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
In the world ye shall have tribulation. We should expect some wind. But be of good cheer. He has overcome.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf of the First Presidency gave hope to those who feel far from shore. In his talk "The Point of Safe Return," from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

Christ came to save us. If we have taken a wrong course, the Atonement of Jesus Christ can give us the assurance that sin is not a point of no return. A safe return is possible if we will follow God's plan for our salvation.
A safe return. The harbor is still there. The tide is still coming in.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time they were lifted after failing. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Peter is restored

blocks.text: Peter had denied the Lord three times on the night He was arrested. Peter wept bitterly. After the Resurrection, Jesus met him by the sea. He did not scold him. He asked him one question, three times. Do you love me? The third time, Peter was grieved.

He saith unto him the third time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? Peter was grieved because he said unto him the third time, Lovest thou me? And he said unto him, Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee. Jesus saith unto him, Feed my sheep.

Three denials, three chances to say yes. The Savior was not shaming Peter. He was restoring him. And then He gave him work to do. Feed my sheep. That is what the Atonement does. It lifts us and sends us back to work.

application.text: Here are some steps for this week.
First, stop pushing alone. Choose one thing that has felt stuck, a habit, a worry, a hurt. Tell the Savior you cannot move it alone, and ask for His help.
Second, step into the water. Take one concrete step this week, such as going to the sacrament with a prepared heart, or repenting of something specific.
Third, answer Peter's question. Ask yourself, Lord, do I love Thee? Then choose one way to show it, and do it before the week is out.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that Jesus Christ is the Son of God and that He lives. I know that His Atonement is real and that it is infinite. I have felt it lift me when I could not lift myself. I know that it is for everyone, and that no one is beyond its reach. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.
